New op-ed in the @idahostatesman on the Jewish High Holy Days, a time of deep reflection as we reflect on the past year in order to do better in the coming one.

This year, 5785 on the Jewish calendar, is particularly painful as it marks a year of disaster, a second Nakba in which the state of Israel has displaced 2 million Palestinians in Gaza, razed cities, killed over 42,000 people, ramped up the violent occupation of the West Bank and courted war with Lebanon, Syria, Iran, and Yemen.

The liturgy of this season instructs us to choose life. In the coming year let’s commit to stopping this genocide and fighting for a future where everyone is free, equal, and safe. In Judaism we say that every life is a universe and to save even one life is to save a world. Let’s mourn the dead and fight for the living.

More than 16,000 Jewish families across Michigan will receive handmade shmurah matzah this year. The initiative, by Chabad Lubavitch of Michigan, enlisted the help of dozens of volunteers to canvass neighborhoods and rural counties to reach every Jew in the state, bringing this special type of matzah — considered ideal for use at the Passover Seder — to Jewish Michiganders. 

The campaign, launched 71 years ago, in 1954 by the Lubavitcher Rebbe, distributes more than one million matzahs in advance of Passover. The Rebbe felt strongly about helping Jews celebrate the Seders with handmade shmurah matzah. 

The state’s 30 Chabad centers and 50 Chabad representative couples chose to ramp up this year’s matzah distribution. “We are hoping we’ll reach every last Jew in the State of Michigan this year, whether they are involved throughout the year or not,” said Rabbi Kasriel Shemtov executive director of Chabad-Lubavitch of Michigan.

Mitzvot in Action! 

Our 7th and 8th graders had a special opportunity to put their Jewish learning into action by joining @chabadofalabama and helping with the mitzvah of building sukkot for families in our Birmingham Jewish community.

This experience was about so much more than building a sukkah. Our students experienced what it means to show up for others and strengthen our community through their own hands and hard work.

They also put two of our NEMJDS Middot into action: Community (Kehillah) and Leadership (Manhigut). Leadership isn’t always about being the person in charge—sometimes it means seeing what needs to be done, stepping forward, and helping make it happen.

We are so proud to see our students learning that mitzvot aren’t just something we study—they are something we do. 

Learning. Leading. Serving. Mitzvot in action.

While many beings communicate and “speak,” there is something special and different about human speech. We have the ability to speak of abstract matters relating to all kinds of intellectual disciplines. We have the ability to convey deep emotions, love, compliments, and our hopes and dreams. We have the ability to speak of practical things, instructions and guidance to others. Unfortunately, we also have the capacity to speak destructively and, G-d forbid, tear another person down.

As we think about the “power” of speech (pun intended), I would encourage us to use the following metric when we set out to speak. Clean. Positive. Kind.

Are the words we choose to use clean? The same mouth that we use to praise Hashem and study Torah must be kept clean of any inappropriate language. 

Are we speaking of positive things or are we using our speech to drag ourselves and our environment down into negativity? Positive speech has the ability to change our surroundings and make them pleasant and energizing. 

Are we using our communication in a kind manner? Are we being constantly critical or are we complimentary? Are we speaking slanderously or being gossipy or are we careful to protect the dignity of others in our manner of speech?

An “articulate soul” is a powerful soul. Words have a major impact, sometimes even greater than sticks or stones. Let us harness our power as a force for good. Through clean, positive, and kind words we can make a real difference in our world, making it a cleaner, more positive, and kinder place, one mouth at a time. 

Shabbat Shalom
Rabbi Mendel Rivkin

Yesterday I got a phone call that seemed like a little gift from heaven. Let me give you some background. Many of you remember Saul Hakim, who passed away last winter. One of his many hobbies was beekeeping. Each Rosh Hashanah he would lovingly provide honey to the community. Within the year before his passing, he moved to New Jersey to live with his son and family. Before he left, he gave his hives to a beekeeper, and he told him that his gift was conditioned on the beekeeper giving honey to the community before Rosh Hashanah. He put the beekeeper in touch with Rabbi Mendy Schechter to ensure that the process would be Kosher.

Yesterday I got the call from Rabbi Schechter that Saul’s hives had produced honey, and it is being made available to the community. Dozens of families will enjoy this gift from heaven and know that even from the next world Saul Hakim loves his people and his community.

As we prepare for Rosh Hashanah tonight, a time that we stand in judgement before Hashem, we would be well served to take a page from Saul’s playbook and demonstrate a love and caring for our brothers and sisters – our fellow Jews. There is no greater pleasure for Hashem our Father, than seeing His children caring for one another.

I hope that everyone has a meaningful Rosh Hashanah. Please make sure to participate in a Shofar blowing service on Sunday.

Wishing you all a Shana Tova, a good and sweet year, a year of health, prosperity, nachas, and meaningful spiritual growth. A year of peace and tranquility in Israel and around the world. Most of all, may this be the year that we finally merit the complete and final redemption through the coming of Mashiach!

Shabbat Shalom and Shana Tova
Rabbi Mendel Rivkin

items.caption:
An Italian comedian did a bit about the contrast in talents of different cultural populations. Imagine going to the emergency room and Dr. Pallazzo comes out to see you, you call out, “got any Leibowitzes back there?” On the other hand, the Jews should get the Italians to cater the Seder, because after breakfast, Jewish cuisine has got nothing…

The cliché of the Jewish doctor! That being said…

This week I underwent a medical procedure. We checked in and I got into the gown and into bed. For a half hour or so, various nurses, techs, and other hospital staff approached to go through the preparatory steps required for the procedure. They were all very nice. As a certain point the doctor entered. He gave me a big smile and said Shalom. We chatted for a minute, and he was very up front about his Jewish identity (not that he could have hidden it from me…). This made me quite comfortable about a procedure that was less than thrilling.

While they were wheeling me to the procedure, the doctor looked in on Malkie in the waiting room and chatted with her. During their conversation, he pulled out his Mezuzah necklace and asked if it meant anything to her. To which she replied with a big smile, “it means Am Yisrael Chai” and then promptly invited him for Shabbos dinner.

During the procedure there were several people in the room. They were all wonderful and professional. I could not be more laudatory about my experience and that is credit to each of them and the role they played. For some reason, I felt a deeper connection with the doctor. At the time, with the sedation kicking in, I was unable to give it much thought. But as I recovered and reflected more on that, I realized that this was a feeling of brotherhood.

There are many good doctors. Contrary to the comedian’s assertion, they can be of any ethnicity. This was not only about the quality of the medical experience. This was about a soul connection. We are both Jewish and we have a shared history, destiny, and soul. 

The comforting feeling of brotherhood escorted me into la la land.

Y’all, the connection is real. We would do well to embrace it!

Shabbat Shalom
Rabbi Mendel Rivkin

It’s a lechi, one of the small but essential pieces that helps form the New Orleans eruv.

Usually, we can’t carry items in a public space on Shabbat. An eruv creates a designated boundary around an area, transforming it into a space that allows carrying within its boundaries.

But keeping an eruv kosher isn’t a “set it and forget it” situation.

Every week, a dedicated group of volunteers, led by Rabbi Yochanan Rivkin, drives around the city, checking the eruv line and making sure every post, wire, fence and lechi is where it needs to be.

Here’s @ycohenchabadno doing his part. 

Because sometimes making Shabbat observance accessible to the community means checking a pole.

Barak Grossberg is a former rocker who grew up in Tel Aviv in a non-observant home deeply immersed in rock music. His father, Shaul Grossberg, was a prominent rock producer in Israel and founder of the Israeli Rock Club.

Life Transformation: In his late teens or early twenties, Barak experienced a powerful spiritual awakening after hearing flute music from Avi Piamenta outside a Chabad house on King George Street in Tel Aviv. That moment inspired his journey toward the Ultra-Orthodox (Chabad) world and shaped his musical direction .

• Keep the Order — Promotes the Seven Laws of Noah; filmed in Kfar Chabad ￼.
 • The Golden Rule — A plea for unity and acceptance, based on the biblical principle “Love your neighbor as yourself” ￼.
 • Lo Meuchar — A reflective pop single about repentance and the choice to pursue joy over suffering ￼.
 • Never Too Late — A heartfelt story told through the music video of a survivor from the Nova Festival attack in Tel Aviv ￼.
 • Hakol Ata — Released before Elul, this song reflects personal struggles and perseverance with gratitude and spiritual growth

items.caption:
Tight Security all around today.  Happy Chanukah.

We are all shaken by the horrific terrorist attack on the 1st Chabad Chanukah candle celebration in Sydney Australia.  I have a personal attachment to Sydney and know some of those involved at the event.  Our condolences go out to those who lost loved ones and we pray for the recovery for those injured. 

Our natural reaction would be to lay low in our own protective places this Chanukah.  But as a Chabad Rabbi I know that doing so is immediate surrender to evil.  I have been more active this morning being in direct contact with Stoughton and Braintree Police Departments to assure that we have the safest possible experience at the South Shore Plaza with K9 officers on site at 2:00, and Stoughton Police escort for our parade at 4:30 starting at Shaloh House Chabad and Menorah lighting at 6:00 at Cobb Corner.  Both departments have been wonderful and most supportive to us. 

Like with the story of Chanukah it was the Maccabees who stood up to the Greeks and liberated the Temple, so too are we being asked to be the Maccabees of today to liberate the dangerous darkness of world with the Light of Chanukah.

Have a very happy and safe Chanukah.

Rabbi Mendel Gurkow

items.caption:
We reached our $50,000 goal, Our $60,000 bonus round has been activated.

Here at Shaloh House Chabad, our hearts are overflowing with gratitude. 

You’ve done something amazing. You recognized that all of our accomplishments – the children who’ve discovered their heritage, the adults making that first connection, the family celebrations, the charity funds distributed –  only came about because we worked together.  You stepped up and grabbed the opportunity.

Yes, that’s us making all the noise outside.
And no, we’re not going home soon.
We Reached our $50,000 Goal. Our $60,000 Bonus Round has been Activated
On behalf of our staff, volunteers, members, families, and the entire community – thank you!

But we’re not done yet; we have entered the bonus round!

The numbers keep growing, at this point we only need $7000.

We’ve all witnessed miracles in our lives in one way or another.  But that doesn’t mean we can just sit back and expect them all the time.  We all must claim our spot in that miracle and do our part.
Go to www.causematch.com/shc

6 hours non stop Chanukah, 3 events, 3 Menorahs and hundreds of people.  At the South Shore Plaza, Stoughton car parade and Cobb Corner.  Thank you to the large and dedicated presence of our police officers securing our safety. 
But I must admit that it was not without a very heavy heart, as reports keep coming in of names of Rabbis and community leaders slain in Sydney, doing the same thing I was doing. 
But they would not want us to stop our Chanukah because of them, but rather make it stronger.  So we did. 
Be sure to do the same.  Light your Menorah every night in celebration.  Help someone else do the same.  We can help you with all you need for Chanukah. 

Have a happy Chanukah.

items.caption:
Camp starts in 51 days! 
Are you kiddos ready for a summer of a lifetime?

Don’t take our word for it!
Listen to what parents are saying about camp! 

My children have been attending Camp Gan Israel for many years, and out of all the camps they’ve experienced in the area, it’s the only one they rave about. What truly sets camp Gan Israel apart is its counselors. They are incredibly responsible, warm, and enthusiastic, and they embody the Jewish pride I want my children to carry. The counselors are passionate about giving my kids a summer they will never forget while instilling meaningful Jewish values. Every year, on the last day of camp, my children sadly say goodbye to their beloved counselors with tears in their eyes. I tell my children, “Don’t be sad that it’s over, be happy that it happened.” 
- Karen Makluf 
My kids loved Camp Gan Israel, and on the last day they cried because it was over. Their countdown to the following July begins as soon as camp ends in August. In addition to the amazing field trips, fun and creative camp activities, kind and thoughtful counselors, and top-notch management, my kids felt a true sense of belonging. They gained Jewish pride—something especially meaningful in today’s world. They learned about Jewish values, but most importantly, they found a community.
My son couldn’t wait to return for his second summer, and my daughter, who had just reached the age requirement, needed no convincing to attend her first summer—she had only heard good things from my son and couldn’t wait. She got what she wanted and more, and has been counting down to her second summer ever since.
My kids still talk about camp and their counselors several times a week, and no other camp has interested them since attending CGI.
-Tal Ron

“Today, we honor the life, legacy, and vision of Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, of blessed memory—one of the most influential Jewish leaders in modern American history. Under his stewardship, this small Hasidic community grew into a global force for faith and service that, after the Holocaust, reinvigorated Judaism worldwide and continues to touch millions of hearts across the globe.”

Today we mark Education and Sharing Day in Buffalo, commemorating 124 years since the birth of the Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem M. Schneerson — a global spiritual leader who championed the power of moral and ethical education to shape strong character and build a more united society.
The Rebbe taught that education is not only about knowledge, but about values — respect, kindness, responsibility, and service to others. His vision of a more peaceful and caring world continues to inspire acts of goodness and kindness, reminding us that even one positive action can create a ripple of change.

Education and Sharing Day is a meaningful opportunity to reflect on our shared responsibility to provide our youth with the tools and values they need to lead purposeful lives and strengthen our community.

We are grateful to Mayor Sean Ryan for recognizing Education and Sharing Day in Buffalo and for supporting initiatives that promote education, unity, and kindness throughout our city.

Let’s take a moment today to do something good — help a neighbor, show extra kindness, and invest in the next generation.

Because when we educate with values, we build a better future.

A devastating tragedy has struck the Jewish community in the United Arab Emirates. Security forces have found the body of Rabbi Zvi Kogan, a resident of Abu Dhabi and manager of the kosher supermarket "Rimon" in Dubai, after he was kidnapped and murdered by an Iranian terrorist cell. 

Rabbi Kogan's disappearance was reported last Thursday, and since then, prayers have been held in Chabad communities around the world. His widow, Rebbetzin Rivka (née Shpilman), is the niece of Rabbi Gabriel Holtzberg, who was murdered in the Mumbai Chabad House 16 years ago. 

The Chabad community is in shock and mourning, and especially Rabbi Kogan's fellow Chabad emissaries around the world, who are preparing for the annual conference of Shluchim later this week. 

May Rabbi Kogan's memory be a blessing, and may his family find comfort in the face of this unbearable tragedy. 

May G-d avenge his blood.

Mom and baby are home and healthy, and Perla, Dovid, and Ita are very excited to welcome their new baby sister!

Nechama is named after her great-great-grandmother, Sarah Nechama Yarmush obm, a woman of deep faith, quiet strength, and unwavering devotion to her family and Judaism. Born into a generation that endured unimaginable challenges, Sarah Nechama carried herself with dignity and resilience. Her home was filled with kindness, tradition, and Torah — where values were lived, not just taught.

She also played a meaningful role in helping bring the teachings of Chassidus to the masses through her work at Kol Menachem, making its depth and beauty accessible to the English-speaking world.

We pray that our Nechama grows up to carry this legacy forward — with strength, purpose, and connection to her heritage. 💗

As we look forward to this year’s Mega Challah Bake, we’re honored to introduce one of the incredible women we’ll be recognizing this year!

𝗠𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗢𝗿𝗹𝘆!

Born and raised in Los Angeles, Orly Cohen came to Ohio for Physician Assistant school, intending to eventually move to warmer weather. However, Hashem had other plans. Thanks to Chabad Young Jewish Professionals in Cincinnati, Orly met lifelong friends and her husband, David. She and David have a one-year-old boy, Eli, who keeps their life fun and exhausting.

Orly always knew she would be a proud member of whatever Jewish community she was involved in. She got her love of hosting from her Brazilian mother, who converted to Judaism because she saw the love and beauty in being Jewish. Orly’s mother has always been known to invite more people than her Shabbat table can hold, but somehow manages to make it look easy.

In high school, Orly was voted most likely to host big Shabbat dinners — a trait she is proud to claim today. She has been very involved in the Chabad YJP community since moving to Cincinnati in 2020. She has served on the Adath Israel Nefesh Board, Moishe House, and as a table host for the Mega Challah Bake.

Orly believes that the best part of being a Jew is having a community of chosen family. She would not have been able to succeed in her professional or personal life without the amazing people she has encountered in the Cincinnati Jewish community. She and David look forward to raising Eli with those same Jewish values.

*𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗦𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁*

As we look forward to this year’s Mega Challah Bake, we’re honored to introduce one of the incredible women we’ll be recognizing this year!

𝗠𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗜𝗳𝗮𝘁!

Israeli born Ifat Lahyani learned from an early age that the heart of a Jewish home is faith, family, hospitality and the warmth of a shared table. These values guide her every day.

Together with her husband, Nadav, and their five children—Noam, Agam, Shoham, Yogev, and Liam—Ifat has created a home where Shabbat and Jewish holidays are celebrated with joy, and where guests are welcomed like family. Throughout the year, she opens her home for Shabbat meals, holiday gatherings, and her annual Mimouna celebration.

One of the defining chapters of Ifat’s life came when she faced cancer. Throughout her journey, faith in Hashem was her greatest source of strength, allowing her to emerge with a renewed sense of purpose, deeper gratitude, and a stronger commitment to a life centered on faith, family and giving to others. Following her recovery, she was blessed with the birth of her youngest son, Liam—a daily reminder that even after life’s greatest challenges, Hashem brings new beginnings and unexpected blessings.

Inspired by that journey, Ifat fulfilled her dream of opening Koriela Kitchen, a kosher bakery and catering company built on Jewish values. Whether baking challah, preparing holiday meals, or catering celebrations, Ifat believes that food has the power to nourish both body and soul, strengthen Jewish identity, and bring people closer together.

Through hospitality and kindness, Ifat hopes to continue inspiring others to celebrate Jewish life, build meaningful connections, and pass these traditions on to future generations.

Want to honor Ifat or one of this year’s other honorees? Place an ad in our Mega Challah Bake event booklet in their honor! Megachallahbakecinci.com

Our Hearts Broken.
Our Resolve Unbreakable.
Light Will Shine Brighter.

​We are devastated and heartbroken by the senseless, barbaric act of terror and murder committed against the Jewish community in Bondi Beach, Australia, during a Chanukah gathering.

​We mourn the brutal loss of Rabbi Eli Schlanger HY’D, the Chabad Rabbi of Bondi Beach, whose life was taken in this unspeakable attack. His memory will forever be a source of strength and light for us.

​Just as the Maccabees faced attempts to extinguish their spiritual flame, we today declare: We refuse to let terror extinguish the light of the Menorah. Their cowardice has and will only fuel our fire of warmth and love.

​Our Response is Clear:
Our planned Chanukah programs will not only continue as scheduled—they will be BIGGER, BRIGHTER, and more public than ever before.

​We call upon every member of our community and all our friends: Come out. Light up the night.

​Join us this Chanukah to show the world, the terrorists, and every voice of darkness that we are not afraid, and the Jewish light will never be diminished.

​We stand in solidarity with Chabad of Bondi Beach and the Jewish community worldwide. Let us turn their darkness into an unprecedented demonstration of light and life!

​Bring a friend.
Bring two.

We are not just carrying on—we are surging forward!

​Am Yisrael Chai!

​May the memory of the righteous be a blessing.
​.
.
#ChanukahStrong #BondiBeach #JewishUnity #AmYisraelChai #LightOverDarkness #NeverAgain #Chanukah

Honoring Mayor Sylvester Turner: A True Champion for Houston

Today, we take a moment to honor the memory of Congressman Sylvester Turner and again express our gratitude for his unwavering dedication to the Houston community. As Mayor, he led with heart, strength, and a deep commitment to making our city a better place for all.

His presence at nearly every City Hall Chanukah Menorah Lighting as Mayor and as Congressman elect stands as testament to his support for Houston’s Jewish community and his belief in the power of unity, faith, and tradition. Through the brightest times and the darkest moments, he has stood with us, embodying the spirit of leadership and inclusion.

His impact on this city is immeasurable and his kindness and devotion will not be forgotten. From all of us—thank you for your service, your friendship, and your light. May your memory be for a blessing.

This week at Hebrew School, we went all the way back to the beginning — Creation!

We discovered what Hashem created on each of the Six Days of Creation, but then went a whole lot deeper:

🌊 Hashem didn’t just create the world once — He is continuously creating it every single moment.

Our younger students brought the Six Days of Creation to life with games and hands-on Creation projects, while our older students explored these big ideas and made their own NeeDoh creations!

What a fantastic first class of the new Hebrew School year!

We kicked off our year by discovering what makes the Torah so special and getting to know its five books, with a special introduction to Bereishis, the first book of the Torah and the focus of our learning this year. ✨

And because learning is always better when you can touch it, experience it (and sometimes eat it! 😉), our students created their own adorable “Torah Is My Guide” mini libraries, complete with all five Chumashim and a special treat connected to each one. 📚🍬

Through games, hands-on activities and lots of discovery, we began exploring an idea we’ll come back to throughout the year:

The Torah isn’t just a book we learn: it’s Hashem’s guide for how we live. 💙

We can’t wait for a year of learning, growing, creating and discovering Bereishis together!

The most wonderful time of the year is here. A time to cherish the moments spent with loved ones, appreciate the blessings that surround us, and reflect on the meaning of Christmas.

Celebrating the birth of Jesus Christ, Christians in Manitoba and around the world rejoice in the profound message of hope and redemption that Christmas brings, and are united in gratitude for the gift of God’s love. Those who follow Christ know that the Christmas season encapsulates his teachings of kindness, peace, and love.

Christmas is also celebrated by many Manitobans of different backgrounds, joining millions of people around the world in adorning communities with colourful lights and decorations, spending time with family, enjoying home-cooked meals, listening to joyous music, watching our favourite holiday classics, and so many wonderful festivities that bring us together.

Most of all, Christmas reminds us about the joy of giving. From exchanging gifts and donating to charity, to random acts of kindness, giving is a hallmark of the season inspired by the compassion that Christ has shown humankind. Manitobans are known for our generosity, so let us support and uplift one another, especially those facing challenges during this time, and offer a lending hand to those less fortunate during and beyond the holidays.

I’d also like to thank those on the front lines—emergency responders, healthcare workers, military personnel, essential service providers, and many more—who have to spend this time away from family or on-call so that their fellow Manitobans can enjoy the holidays.

As we look to the future, may the coming year bring prosperity, good health, and happiness to every corner of our beautiful province.

On behalf of our PC Caucus and our families, we wish all Manitobans a very merry Christmas, a safe and happy holiday, and the very best in the new year.

At sunset tonight, Jewish communities across Manitoba and the world will light the first candles of the Hanukkah menorah, celebrating the triumph of light over darkness.

More than 2,000 years ago, Jewish warriors rose up against their oppressors who had outlawed Judaism in the holy land and destroyed the Temple of Jerusalem. The successful liberation of the Jewish people and rededication of the Second Temple is commemorated through Hanukkah.

History has witnessed Jewish resilience and perseverance time and time again. We have seen it in 200 BCE, and we see it now in 2023 CE. We know that the recent rise in antisemitism has made many Jewish households unsure if they can celebrate Hanukkah safely or proudly display their identity in public. There is also ongoing pain caused by the Israel-Hamas conflict.

The spirit of Hanukkah tells us that hope will prevail over adversity. We urge all Manitobans to stand up in the face of anti-Jewish hate to help our fellow Manitobans kindle the light and overcome darkness.

May the glow of the menorah burn bright and bring warmth to you this Hanukkah.

Chag sameach!

A Sofer (scribe) visited @bethmenachemchabad today to check our mezuzot! 

🤔Did you know? Every mezuzah is a scroll with the Shema handwritten by a Sofer with a special quill and ink on kosher parchment, in 22 lines. If even one letter is missing, cracked or touching another, the mezuzah is no longer kosher.

A mezuzah should be checked by a Sofer twice every seven years. On the back of every mezuzah is G-d’s name Sha-dai, which stands for “Guardian of the doors of Israel” 🚪

When was yours last checked? Reach out to us and we’ll help!
